newsitem.title: USA: US CORP BONDS- Treasury selloff sidelines players.
newsitem.headline: US CORP BONDS- Treasury selloff sidelines players.

text.p: Corporate bond players took to the sidelines Friday as a batch of strong U.S. economic data triggered a sell-off in U.S. Treasuries, dealers said.
"The market got crushed so that put an end to our buyers," said one high-grade trader. "There really hasn't been much flow ... players weren't showing much paper today."
"People are underwater right now ... I think we'll see a better indication on Monday," he said. "When we did see same paper offered though, it was at tighter levels."
Stronger-than-expected readings on the U.S. employment and maanufacturing fronts triggerd over a two-point drop in the benchmark U.S. 30-year Treasury bond on Friday.

Earlier, the Labor Department reported an increase of 316,000 in July payrolls and a drop to 4.8 percent in the unemployment rate. Later followed by a 58.6 reading in the manufacturing activity index of the the National Association of Purchasing Management.
The T-bond ended the day sharply lower, closing off 67/32 at 102-7/32 to yield 6.46 percent versus 6.30 percent at Thursday's close.

The offering will include five, 10 and 30-year maturities. Morgan Stanley Dean Witter, Credit Suisse First Boston and Bear Stearns & Co Inc will jointly lead-manager the deal; however, Morgan Stanley will act as book running lead manager, the company said.
Players said, higher interest rates new government supply slated for next week should keep other issuers away.
The U.S. Treasury is slated to sell $16 billion in three-year notes, $12 billion in 10-year notes and $10 billion in 30-year bonds next week.
Issuers anticipating a possible change in market tone; given the key data, capitilized on lower interest rates earlier in the week, to bring over $5.0 billion in new high-grade debt.
A recent rally in the U.S. bond market had seen the yield on the benchmark 30-year bond drop from a 6.71 percent close on July 2, to 6.30 percent at the close on July 31.
No new investment grade issues were seen Friday, as issuers retreated to the sidelines with rates turning higher.
Looking ahead, Raytheon Co's is slated to issue a $2.5 million three-part debt offering next week.
In other news, U.S. high-yield bond mutual funds received net cash inflows of $379.9 million in the latest recorded week, which ended July 30, according to AMG Data Services.
Next week's high-yield business is expected to include at least 20 new junk deals totalling about $3.0 billion.
Turning to the secondary junk arena, prices ended off 1/4 to 1/2 but U.S. Treasury and stock markets were the focus of the session, players said.
"Our market wasn't off that much ... we really didn't see many accounts come in to sell in this market; government's were the main show today," one high-yield trader said.
Seperately, Grand Union debt rebounded, gaining 8-1/2 points to trade at 49 bid, 50 offer, despite a downgrade to the company's credit by Moody's Investors Service.
Moody's cut Grand Union's bank facility rating to B3 from B2 and its senior unsecured bonds due 2004, to Caa3 from Caa1.

On Thursday, the company said its preliminary first quarter results are below company expectations and result in a technical financial covenant default under its bank lending agreement. The company said it had not missed any payments to its bankers, bondholders or vendors.
